# My remote key fob only works a foot from my door

If your 2006 Chevy Impala's remote key fob fails to unlock, lock, or pop the trunk until you are roughly a foot away from the driver's side, and if remote start is completely dead even when seated inside the vehicle, the issue has moved beyond a simple battery replacement. While swapping the CR2032 battery is the first logical step for any RF device, the symptoms you are describingâspecifically the drastic reduction in effective range and the intermittent internal responseâpoint to a failure in the transceiver chain or a corrupted handshake protocol that re-syncing cannot fix.

In automotive electronics, the "sync" process typically involves resetting the rolling code algorithm within the vehicle's Body Control Module (BCM) to match the fob's current counter state. If you have already performed this re-sync procedure on two different units and the result is consistent failure at short range, the radio receiver inside the Impala is likely saturated with interference or has suffered a hardware degradation common in vehicles of that era. The 2006 model year often utilized older antenna designs that are prone to corrosion or breakage due to vibration fatigue over time. When the antenna coil degrades, the signal-to-noise ratio drops significantly. A strong signal from your fob can no longer be distinguished from background noise until you physically place the fob right next to the receiver, explaining why it works at one foot but fails at ten.

The behavior where the remote start clicks but does not engage is particularly telling. That click is the BCM acknowledging the RF burst and validating the security handshake, but the subsequent silence indicates that the command never reached the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) or that the PCM rejected the request due to a safety interlock. In many GM platforms of this generation, the system checks for valid door-open/closed signals, brake pedal position, and neutral gear status via CAN bus messages before energizing the starter relay. If the BCM itself is failing to broadcast these status messages correctlyâoften a side effect of the same antenna or module failureâthe PCM will time out the request after the initial acknowledgement click.

Re-syncing the fob assumes that the vehicle's receiver is functioning perfectly. It does not repair a broken antenna coil, nor does it fix a BCM microcontroller that is struggling to process incoming signals amidst electrical noise. Since you have already replaced batteries and re-synced multiple units, continuing to attempt synchronization will yield diminishing returns. The most reliable technical solution at this stage is to replace the entire Body Control Module or, in some configurations, the specific radio receiver module integrated into the BCM.

There is a nuance regarding aftermarket fobs versus OEM replacements. If you are using third-party clones, ensure they utilize the same frequency (typically 315 MHz for North American GM vehicles of that era) and protocol. However, even with compatible hardware, if the vehicle's receiver sensitivity has degraded due to age or environmental factors, no amount of software re-calibration will restore full-range functionality. The only way to definitively rule out a bad fob is to have a dealer diagnose the BCM's antenna integrity, but given the two-fob failure pattern, the fault lies squarely with the vehicle's transmission side of the link.

If you require a long-term solution that bypasses the failing internal hardware without a full module replacement, you might consider installing an aftermarket wireless entry system. These systems often use more modern receivers with external antennas mounted in locations optimized for signal strength, effectively upgrading the radio subsystem entirely. This approach separates the RF reception logic from the aging BCM electronics, providing a robust fix that addresses both the range issue and the communication latency causing the remote start failure.
